title: At least eight dead after Brooklyn apartment building collapses into construction pit
excerpt: At least eight people were killed after a three-story Brooklyn apartment building collapsed into a construction pit next door, with rescue crews still searching the rubble.
content:
At least eight people were confirmed dead early Thursday after a three-story apartment building in Brooklyn collapsed into an open construction pit next door, and rescue crews were still searching the rubble for survivors.

The building at 1321 Flatbush Ave., in the Flatbush section of Brooklyn, fell into the construction site next door at 2625 Bedford Ave. shortly after 4 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 11. The Fire Department of New York said it received the call at 4:01 p.m. and units arrived within one minute.

The death toll rose through the morning. Six bodies were pulled from the rubble overnight, and two more people died after being taken to a hospital, the New York Post reported early Thursday. On Wednesday night, officials had confirmed two deaths and 17 injuries.

At least 19 other people were injured, four of them critically, according to the Post's updated reporting. Seven children were among the injured. Firefighters pulled several survivors from the wreckage alive Wednesday evening, including a woman and her two children, ages 7 and 2, and a pregnant woman. At least three firefighters were injured during the rescue effort.

More than 250 fire and emergency medical workers responded, with 69 units and search dogs working the pile. Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said Wednesday night that crews did not know how many people might still be in the collapse zone, and officials warned the toll would likely keep rising. The search was expected to stretch for days.

The building was a three-story mixed-use structure with a store at street level and four apartments above it. The lot next door was being prepared for a new building: city Department of Buildings filings show a January 2026 application for a nine-story mixed-use building with a cellar, filed for the owner, W6 Facility X LLC. Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said construction crews had been excavating the site next door when the building crumbled into it.

Officials have not given a cause. The Department of Buildings and law enforcement agencies are investigating, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined city officials at a late-night briefing. The records do not explain the collapse, and officials have not tied it to the work at the site.

Displaced residents were taken to a reception center at the Flatbush YMCA, 1401 Flatbush Ave., where the Red Cross registered 12 adults and helped find places for them to spend the night. Flatbush Avenue was closed between Clarendon Avenue and Bedford Avenue while rescue work continued.

Update — November 13, 2026

Rescue operations at the collapse site ended Thursday afternoon, November 12. The Fire Department announced at 3:37 p.m. Eastern that it had concluded its search and determined there were no more victims at the site, and the site was turned over to the Department of Buildings and the Police Department. The death toll stands at eight: six adults, including two construction workers, and two children — a 9-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, according to the Police Department. Six of the victims died at the scene and two died after being taken to hospitals. Eighteen people were injured, 14 civilians and four firefighters; one person remained in critical condition Thursday afternoon and most of the others were in stable condition, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at a midday news conference. Full vacate orders were issued for the collapsed building and three neighboring buildings at 1323, 1325 and 1327 Flatbush Avenue. The mayor also ordered safety inspections at about 100 construction sites linked to five entities tied to the neighboring project, and the Brooklyn District Attorney's Office joined the investigation. The cause of the collapse has still not been determined; the city's buildings commissioner said construction workers were excavating the adjacent site when the building fell. The Red Cross registered seven households — 14 adults and five children — for assistance.

Update — November 15, 2026

Police on Thursday evening released the names of all eight people killed in the collapse: Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Barry Mamadou, 23; Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26; Edgar Sapon, 26; Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31; and Ndiaye Mamadou, 31. Two of the dead were construction workers at the neighboring site. The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office has opened a criminal investigation into whether criminal conduct contributed to the collapse, The New York Times reported Friday; no charges have been filed, and an investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing. The Department of Buildings retracted an early finding blaming unsafe construction at the adjacent site after Crain's New York Business asked about it, saying the cause remains under investigation. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Friday the city has expanded its inspection sweep to more than 160 construction sites linked to six entities tied to the project, up from about 100, and has hired an outside engineering firm for an independent report on the collapse, the Associated Press reported.

Update — November 17, 2026

New reporting on the companies tied to the neighboring construction site has sharpened the picture of their enforcement histories, though the cause of the collapse still has not been determined and no charges have been filed. The demolition contractor at 2625 Bedford Avenue, N Tech Design of America, received 305 penalties across 139 job sites over four years, according to city hearing records reviewed by The Real Deal, and many remained open and unpaid as of November 16. The same company had two prior violations at the Bedford Avenue site itself: in March, the Department of Buildings found inadequate overhead protection during demolition and issued a stop-work order, drawing a $2,500 penalty; in April, inspectors found the crew had kept tearing the building down anyway, drawing a $10,000 penalty. The penalties were later paid in full and the order was lifted in May. Separately, Realtor.com reported that Townhouse Builders Inc., doing business as Promont and the general contractor for the excavation work, has been sued at least 67 times since 2012, including a 2020 lawsuit in Kings County Supreme Court alleging it compromised the structural integrity of nearby properties during an excavation; that suit seeks more than $1.1 million, remains open, and has its next hearing in January 2027. The Real Deal also reported that the owner of the collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, Olufemi Falade, had nearly 100 housing violations at the building before it fell and had served jail time in 2006 over conditions across his Brooklyn portfolio. The Brooklyn District Attorney’s criminal investigation and the city’s independent engineering review are continuing.

Update — November 22, 2026

The city has ordered the demolition of the neighboring building at 1323 Flatbush Avenue, which engineers found too unstable to shore up, the Department of Buildings said; tenants cannot return for their belongings, in part because of asbestos contamination, and crews must first brace 1325 Flatbush Avenue, which remains under a vacate order. A tenant of the collapsed building, Dengane Omari Jack, has sued the building’s owner, the site’s owners, the contractors and the engineer who drew the excavation plan, saying he photographed cracks near the building’s entrance in October and reported them, Gothamist reported. A Department of Buildings inspection blitz has halted work at five sites tied to the engineer and a special inspector, Gothamist reported. NBC New York reported that the engineer who drew the excavation plan had twice been appointed to help revise the city’s construction code and had faced four lawsuits over damage to neighboring buildings, none of which found him responsible. At a vigil at the site on November 21, Brenda Vásquez, whose husband Edgar Sapón died in the collapse, said “there was someone who failed to supervise that work,” the New York Post reported. The cause of the collapse still has not been determined, and the Brooklyn District Attorney’s criminal investigation continues; no charges have been filed.

Update — November 27, 2026

Lawsuits filed since the November 11 collapse blame the disaster on inadequate shoring and underpinning at the excavation next door, the Associated Press reported on November 20. A lawsuit filed by five injured construction workers says the dig at 2625 Bedford Ave. lacked adequate retaining walls, shoring and underpinning to keep the adjoining building safe, and that excavation continued even after the building’s facade began to crack. Other lawsuits blame the construction site’s owner and contractors, the engineering firm that drew up the excavation plan, and the owner of the building that collapsed. The death toll remains eight, the cause has still not been determined, and the Brooklyn District Attorney’s investigation continues. On November 25, the city’s Department of Buildings said it had retained LERA Consulting Structural Engineers to conduct the independent forensic investigation it promised after the collapse, Engineering News-Record reported. The city is also checking more than 160 construction sites tied to companies involved in the project.
